topics.title: Personal Pronouns
topics.description: Learn ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, Sie and their usage

topics.title: Present Tense Verbs
topics.description: Conjugate regular and common irregular verbs in the present tense — and master the V2 rule that governs every German sentence

lessons.title: Präsens — What It Is and When to Use It
lessons.shortDescription: The German present tense covers both 'I do' and 'I am doing' — and the conjugated verb always sits in position 2, no exceptions.

sections.title: Das Präsens — Germany's Most-Used Tense
sections.content: Präsens is the present tense and the most important tense in everyday German. Unlike English, German does not separate 'I learn' from 'I am learning' — both are simply Ich lerne Deutsch. This single tense covers what English expresses with two: the simple present and the present continuous. This is actually good news: one tense to learn instead of two.

sections.title: The 4 Main Uses of Präsens
items: 1. Current actions — something happening right now: Ich esse gerade. (I am eating right now.)
2. Habits and repeated actions — things done regularly: Ich trainiere jeden Tag. (I train every day.)
3. General facts and truths — permanent or universal truths: Die Erde ist rund. (The earth is round.)
4. Near future — when the time is specified, Präsens replaces the future tense: Morgen fahre ich nach Toronto. (Tomorrow I am going to Toronto.)

sections.title: One German Tense = Two English Tenses
sections.content: Ich lerne Deutsch has two valid English translations: 'I learn German' (habit/ongoing) and 'I am learning German' (happening now). German does not distinguish between them — context tells you which meaning is intended. This is one of the first adjustments English speakers must make when learning German.

sections.title: Sentence Structure: The V2 Rule
sections.content: The single most important word order rule in German: the conjugated verb always occupies Position 2 in a main clause. It is never in position 1 or position 3. Position 1 can be the subject, a time adverb, or any other element — but the verb immediately follows in position 2, and the subject moves after it if necessary. Formula: Position 1 + conjugated verb + rest of sentence.

sections.title: Sentence Analysis: Ich lerne heute Deutsch
Inversion: When the Subject Is Not First
sections.content: When anything other than the subject starts the sentence (a time word, place, adverb), the verb still holds position 2 — the subject moves to position 3. This is called inversion and is mandatory in German. Wrong: Heute ich lerne Deutsch. Right: Heute lerne ich Deutsch. (Today I learn German.) The verb lerne never moves — it is always position 2.

sections.title: The V2 Rule with Different Position-1 Elements
sections.content: Subject first (normal): Ich lerne heute Deutsch. | Time word first (inversion): Heute lerne ich Deutsch. | Place first (inversion): In Berlin lerne ich Deutsch. | Adverb first (inversion): Gern lerne ich Deutsch. Notice that lerne is always in position 2 regardless of what starts the sentence.

vocabulary.example: Ich lerne Deutsch. (I learn / am learning German.)
Ich esse gerade. (I am eating right now.)
Ich trainiere jeden Tag. (I train every day.)
Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. (Tomorrow I am going to Berlin.)
Er arbeitet heute nicht. (He is not working today.)
Heute gehe ich zur Arbeit. (Today I am going to work.)

exercises.question: How do you express both 'I learn German' and 'I am learning German' in German?

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch / Ich bin lernend Deutsch
options.explanation: 'Ich bin lernend' is technically possible but almost never used in natural spoken German.

options.text: Both are simply: Ich lerne Deutsch.
options.explanation: Correct! German Präsens covers both English meanings. Context tells you which is intended.

options.text: They are two different tenses in German too
options.explanation: No — German Präsens is one tense that covers both English present simple and present continuous.

exercises.explanation: German Präsens = English simple present + present continuous. One form, two English meanings.

exercises.question: Which sentence correctly applies the V2 rule?

options.explanation: Wrong! After 'Heute' (position 1), the verb must come next (position 2), then the subject.
Correct! Heute (pos. 1) + gehe (pos. 2) + ich (pos. 3). Verb is always position 2.
Wrong! The verb cannot go to the end in a main clause. V2 rule: verb is always position 2.

exercises.explanation: V2 rule: the conjugated verb is ALWAYS position 2. When something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves to position 3.

exercises.question: 'Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin' uses Präsens to express a future action.

options.explanation: Correct! German uses Präsens for the near future when a time marker (like 'morgen') makes the future meaning clear.
Actually true — this is Präsens use #4. 'Morgen' signals the future, so Präsens works perfectly.

exercises.explanation: Präsens use #4: near future with a time marker. Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin = Tomorrow I am going to Berlin.

exercises.instruction: Which use of Präsens is this?
exercises.question: Die Erde ist rund. (The earth is round.)

options.explanation: The earth being round is not a current action — it is always true.
Habits involve a person doing something regularly. This is a universal truth.
Correct! Die Erde ist rund is a permanent, universal fact — Präsens use #3.
No time marker for future here — the earth being round is a timeless truth.

exercises.explanation: Präsens use #3: general facts. Die Erde ist rund — always true, no time reference needed.

lessons.title: Regular Verb Conjugation — Stamm + Endung
lessons.shortDescription: Learn the system behind regular German verb conjugation: remove -en from any infinitive to get the Stamm, then add the correct Endung for each subject.

sections.title: Der Infinitiv — The Base Form of Every Verb
sections.content: Every German verb has an infinitive — its base, unconjugated form. German infinitives almost always end in -en (lernen, machen, fahren) or occasionally just -n (sammeln, wandern). In a dictionary, verbs are always listed in the infinitive. When you use a verb in a sentence, you must conjugate it — change it to match the subject.

sections.title: Stamm and Endung — The Two Parts of Every Regular Verb
sections.content: To conjugate a regular German verb, split the infinitive into two parts: Stamm (stem — the root that carries the meaning and stays constant) and Endung (ending — what changes depending on the subject). The formula is: Infinitiv minus -en = Stamm. Then add the correct ending for the subject. Example: lernen → lern (Stamm) + correct ending.

sections.title: Two More Regular Verbs: machen and kaufen
Special Case: Verbs Ending in -ten and -den
sections.content: When the Stamm ends in -t or -d (arbeit-, find-, red-), an extra -e is inserted before the endings -st and -t to make pronunciation possible. Without it, 'arbeittest' would be unpronounceable. So: arbeiten → du arbeitest (not 'arbeitst'), er arbeitet (not 'arbeitt'). Similarly: finden → du findest, er findet.

sections.title: Regular Verbs in Real Sentences
sections.content: Ich spiele Fußball. (I play football.) | Du kaufst das Buch. (You are buying the book.) | Er macht die Hausaufgaben. (He does the homework.) | Wir lernen jeden Tag Deutsch. (We learn German every day.) | Ihr arbeitet viel zu viel! (You work way too much!)

vocabulary.example: Ich lerne jeden Tag. (I learn every day.)
Er macht die Arbeit. (He does the work.)
Wir spielen Fußball. (We play football.)
Sie kauft ein Buch. (She buys a book.)
Ihr arbeitet heute? (Are you working today?)
Ich frage den Lehrer. (I ask the teacher.)
Er wohnt in München. (He lives in Munich.)
Sie kommen morgen. (They are coming tomorrow.)

exercises.instruction: Fill in the correct Präsens form.
exercises.question: Du ___ jeden Tag Deutsch. (You learn German every day.) [lernen]
exercises.explanation: lernen → Stamm: lern- + du ending (-st) = lernst. Du lernst jeden Tag Deutsch.

exercises.question: What is the correct conjugation of 'arbeiten' for 'er'?

options.explanation: Not a real German form. The stem 'arbeit-' ends in -t, so an extra -e is inserted before the personal ending.
Correct! arbeit- + extra -e + -t = arbeitet. The -e is inserted because the stem ends in -t.
Missing the personal ending entirely. The form is: arbeit + e + t = arbeitet.
That is the ich form (arbeit + -e). For er/sie/es, the ending is -(e)t.

exercises.explanation: Verbs with a stem ending in -t or -d insert an extra -e before -st and -t: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.

exercises.question: What is the Stamm (stem) of the verb 'spielen'?

options.explanation: That is the full infinitive. The Stamm is what you get after removing -en.
Correct! spielen minus -en = spiel. All conjugations are built on this stem.
That is the ich form (spiel + -e). The Stamm itself is just 'spiel'.
That is the er/sie/es form (spiel + -t). The Stamm is just 'spiel'.

exercises.explanation: Stamm = Infinitiv minus -en. spielen → spiel. Then: ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen.

exercises.instruction: Fill in the correct form of 'machen'.
exercises.question: Ihr ___ heute Hausaufgaben. (You are doing homework today.)
exercises.explanation: machen → Stamm: mach- + ihr ending (-t) = macht. Note: ihr and er/sie/es both use -t; the subject makes the meaning clear.

lessons.title: Irregular Verbs — Stem Vowel Changes
lessons.shortDescription: Many high-frequency German verbs change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms. Learn the three patterns: a→ä, e→ie, and e→i.

sections.title: Unregelmäßige Verben — What Makes a Verb Irregular
sections.content: Irregular (unregelmäßig) verbs use the same personal endings as regular verbs — the endings themselves (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en) do not change. What changes is the vowel inside the stem, but only for the second person singular (du) and third person singular (er/sie/es). The other four forms — ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie — keep the original stem vowel and conjugate exactly like regular verbs.

sections.title: The Three Main Stem Vowel Change Patterns
fahren (a→ä) — Full Conjugation
rows: I drive / go — original stem, no change
we drive — original stem, no change
you (pl.) drive — original stem, no change

sections.title: Only du and er/sie/es Change — All Others Stay Regular
sections.content: This is the most important thing to remember: only the du form and the er/sie/es form get the changed vowel. All other forms — ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie — use the original stem and follow the normal pattern. You only need to memorize two special forms per verb, not six.

sections.title: nehmen and essen Are Extra Irregular
sections.content: nehmen and essen go beyond a simple vowel swap: nehmen → du nimmst, er nimmt (the entire consonant cluster changes). essen → du isst, er isst (the -ss merges with the -st ending). Both must be memorized individually — they cannot be predicted from the pattern alone. Both are extremely high-frequency verbs.

sections.title: Irregular Verbs in Natural Sentences
sections.content: Ich fahre nach Berlin. (I am going to Berlin.) vs. Du fährst nach Berlin. (You are going to Berlin.) | Er liest ein Buch. (He is reading a book.) | Sie spricht sehr gut Deutsch! (She speaks German very well!) | Was isst du gern? (What do you like to eat?) | Er nimmt den Bus. (He takes the bus.)

vocabulary.example: Ich fahre nach Berlin. Du fährst auch?
Er schläft bis 10 Uhr. (He sleeps until 10 o'clock.)
Sie läuft jeden Morgen. (She runs every morning.)
Er liest jeden Abend. (He reads every evening.)
Siehst du das? (Do you see that?)
Sie spricht drei Sprachen. (She speaks three languages.)
Er nimmt die U-Bahn. (He takes the underground.)
Was gibst du mir? (What are you giving me?)
Was isst du gern? (What do you like to eat?)

exercises.question: Er ___ ein Buch. (He is reading a book.)

options.explanation: lest is the ihr form. For er/sie/es, lesen has the e→ie change.
lesen is the infinitive or wir/sie form, not the er form.
Correct! lesen → e→ie for er/sie/es: liest. Er liest ein Buch.
lese is the ich form. For er/sie/es the vowel changes: e→ie → liest.

exercises.explanation: lesen is an e→ie irregular verb. Only du and er/sie/es get the changed vowel: du liest, er liest.

exercises.instruction: Fill in the correct form of 'fahren'.
exercises.question: Du ___ morgen nach Wien. (You are going to Vienna tomorrow.)
exercises.hint: fahren: a→ä change for du. Stem changes to fähr-, then add the du ending -st.
exercises.explanation: fahren → a→ä for du: fähr- + -st = fährst. Du fährst morgen nach Wien.

exercises.question: Which forms of a stem-vowel irregular verb get the changed vowel?

options.explanation: Only two forms change — the rest stay with the original stem vowel.
The ich form never changes in stem-vowel irregular verbs.
Correct! Only the 2nd and 3rd person singular get the changed vowel. All other forms keep the original stem.
These plural forms always keep the original stem vowel.

exercises.explanation: Stem vowel changes apply ONLY to du and er/sie/es. Ich, wir, ihr, sie/Sie always use the original stem.

lessons.title: sein and haben — The Two Essential Verbs
lessons.shortDescription: sein (to be) and haben (to have) are completely irregular and must be memorized — they appear in every single German conversation and form the basis of all past tenses.

sections.title: Why sein and haben Are Special
sections.content: sein and haben are the two highest-frequency verbs in German. They are completely irregular — they do not follow the Stamm + Endung pattern at all and must be memorized directly. Beyond their standalone meanings (to be, to have), they are the two auxiliary verbs used to form the Perfekt (conversational past tense), making them even more essential. Every single German conversation uses both of these verbs multiple times.

sections.title: sein — Full Präsens Conjugation
rows: Er ist Arzt. (He is a doctor.)

sections.title: haben — Full Präsens Conjugation
rows: Ich habe ein Auto. (I have a car.)
Hast du Zeit? (Do you have time?)
Wir haben eine Frage. (We have a question.)

sections.title: haben for Physical and Emotional States
sections.content: German uses haben (to have) for many states that English expresses with 'to be': Ich habe Hunger. (I am hungry — literally 'I have hunger'). Ich habe Durst. (I am thirsty). Ich habe Angst. (I am afraid). Ich habe Lust. (I feel like it). Ich habe Recht. (I am right). Ich habe Glück. (I am lucky). These are fixed expressions — do not substitute sein for haben in these phrases.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Their Corrections
rows: Infinitive used — verb must match subject
V2 rule broken — verb must be position 2
sein used for possession — use haben

sections.title: Präsens — Complete Summary
sections.content: You now have all the tools for German Präsens: 1) Regular verbs: Stamm + correct Endung (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en). 2) Verbs with -t/-d stems: insert an extra -e before -st and -t. 3) Stem-vowel irregular verbs: only du and er/sie/es change (a→ä, e→ie, e→i). 4) sein and haben: fully irregular, memorize directly. 5) V2 rule: the conjugated verb is always position 2, no exceptions.

vocabulary.example: Ich bin müde. Du bist nett. Er ist hier.
Ich habe Zeit. Er hat Hunger. Wir haben Glück.
Ich bin müde. (I am tired.)
Er hat Hunger. (He is hungry.)
Ich habe Durst. (I am thirsty.)
Sie hat Angst. (She is afraid.)
Du hast Recht! (You are right!)
Ihr habt Glück! (You are lucky!)

exercises.instruction: Fill in the correct form of 'sein'.
exercises.question: Wir ___ heute sehr müde. (We are very tired today.)
exercises.hint: sein is completely irregular. What is the wir form?
exercises.explanation: sein: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. The wir form is sind.

exercises.question: How do you say 'He is hungry' in German?

options.explanation: German uses haben for physical states like hunger, not sein.
Close but wrong. In German: Er hat Hunger (noun) — not 'hat hungrig' (adjective with haben).
Correct! Hunger is a noun in German. 'He has hunger' = Er hat Hunger = He is hungry.
Er ist hungrig exists but is less natural. The common idiomatic expression is always Er hat Hunger.

exercises.explanation: Physical states in German use haben: Hunger haben (be hungry), Durst haben (be thirsty), Angst haben (be afraid), Glück haben (be lucky).

exercises.question: Ihr ___ viel Glück! (You are very lucky!)

options.explanation: Correct! haben for ihr: habt. Ihr habt viel Glück!
haben is the wir/sie/Sie form. The ihr form is habt.
hat is the er/sie/es form. The ihr form is habt.
hast is the du form. The ihr form is habt.

exercises.explanation: haben: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. The ihr form is habt.

exercises.question: 'Heute ich arbeite' is a correct German sentence.

options.explanation: Wrong! This breaks the V2 rule. After 'Heute' (position 1), the verb must be position 2: Heute arbeite ich.
Correct — it is wrong! V2 rule: Heute (pos. 1) + arbeite (pos. 2) + ich (pos. 3) → Heute arbeite ich.

exercises.explanation: V2 rule: verb is always position 2. When 'Heute' starts the sentence, the subject 'ich' moves after the verb: Heute arbeite ich.

lessons.title: The 20 Most Essential German Verbs
lessons.shortDescription: Master the 20 highest-frequency German verbs — from sein and haben to everyday action verbs.

sections.title: Why Start with Verbs?
sections.content: Statistical analysis of real German conversations shows that just 20 verbs account for a huge proportion of everything Germans say. Every sentence needs a verb — and these 20 are the ones you will encounter in every single conversation, every day. Before memorizing noun lists, master these verbs and you will have the skeleton of the language.

sections.title: sein — To Be (Rank #1, the Most Important Word in German)
sections.content: sein is the most frequently used word in the entire German language. It describes who you are, how you feel, your profession, nationality, and location. It is highly irregular — there is no shortcut. You must memorize all its forms directly from the start.

sections.title: sein — Full Present Tense (Präsens)
rows: Er ist Arzt. (He is a doctor.)

sections.title: haben — To Have (Rank #2)
sections.content: haben expresses possession and is also the auxiliary verb used to form the Perfekt tense (conversational past) with most verbs. Together, sein and haben are the two pillars of German grammar — they appear in almost every conversation and every tense.

sections.title: haben — Full Present Tense (Präsens)
rows: Er hat ein Auto. (He has a car.)

sections.title: Native Speaker Tip: haben for Physical States
sections.content: Unlike English, German uses haben (to have) for physical and emotional states: Ich habe Hunger (I am hungry — literally 'I have hunger'), Ich habe Durst (I am thirsty), Ich habe Angst (I am afraid), Ich habe Lust (I feel like it). This is one of the most common translation traps for English speakers and must be memorized as fixed phrases.

sections.title: Modal Verbs: können, müssen, wollen (Ranks 4, 5, 6)
sections.content: Modal verbs modify the meaning of other verbs and appear constantly in daily speech. The key grammar rule: the modal verb takes position 2 in the sentence, and the main verb goes to the END as an infinitive. Example: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen. (I can speak German.) — sprechen goes to the very end.

sections.title: The Three Core Modal Verbs
rows: Ich kann das machen. (I can do that.)
Ability and possibility — the most versatile modal verb
Ich muss arbeiten. (I have to work.)
Strong obligation; muss nicht = don't have to (NOT must not!)
Ich will nach Hause gehen. (I want to go home.)
Strong intention or wish — not polite for requests, use möchten instead

sections.title: Critical Trap: muss nicht ≠ must not
sections.content: Ich muss nicht does NOT mean 'I must not' — it means 'I do not have to' (no obligation). To say 'I must not / I am not allowed to', use: ich darf nicht. Compare: Du musst nicht kommen. (You do not have to come.) vs. Du darfst nicht rauchen. (You must not smoke.) This distinction trips up nearly every English speaker.

sections.title: werden — A Verb with Three Jobs (Rank #3)
sections.content: werden has three uses: 1) Main verb meaning 'to become': Er wird Arzt. (He is becoming a doctor.) 2) Future auxiliary: Ich werde kommen. (I will come.) 3) Passive voice auxiliary: Das Haus wird gebaut. (The house is being built.) At A1 level, focus on meanings 1 and 2.

sections.title: High-Frequency Action Verbs (Ranks 7–20)
rows: Was machst du? (What are you doing?)
Was sagst du? (What are you saying?)
Wir gehen nach Hause. (We are going home.)
Kommst du mit? (Are you coming along?)
Ich weiß es nicht. (I do not know.)
Ich kenne Berlin gut. (I know Berlin well.)
Siehst du das? (Do you see that?)
Sprechen Sie Deutsch? (Do you speak German?)
Wie findest du das? (What do you think of it?)
Gibst du mir das Buch? (Will you give me the book?)
Ich nehme den Bus. (I take the bus.)
Ich arbeite heute nicht. (I am not working today.)
Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?)

sections.title: wissen vs. kennen — Two Ways to Say 'Know'
sections.content: German has two verbs for 'to know': wissen is for facts and information — things you know in your mind: Ich weiß, dass er kommt. (I know that he is coming.) Ich weiß es nicht. (I do not know.) kennen is for people, places, and things you are personally familiar with: Ich kenne ihn. (I know him.) Kennst du Berlin? (Do you know Berlin?) Mixing these is the single most common vocabulary mistake at A1 level.

sections.title: A Real Conversation Using These 20 Verbs
sections.content: — Hallo! Ich bin Anna. Kennst du Berlin? — Ja, ich kenne es gut. Ich wohne hier seit drei Jahren. Ich arbeite bei einer Firma in Mitte. — Was machst du dort? — Ich spreche mit Kunden und mache Präsentationen. Ich muss jeden Tag früh kommen. — Kannst du heute Abend kommen? Wir wollen zusammen essen gehen. — Ich weiß nicht... Ich habe viel Arbeit heute. Aber ich will kommen, wenn ich kann.

vocabulary.example: Ich bin hier. (I am here.)
Ich habe Zeit. (I have time.)
Er wird Arzt. (He is becoming a doctor.)
Ich kann Deutsch sprechen. (I can speak German.)
Ich muss jetzt gehen. (I have to go now.)
Ich will Deutsch lernen. (I want to learn German.)
Was machst du? (What are you doing?)
Ich sage die Wahrheit. (I am telling the truth.)
Wir gehen jetzt. (We are going now.)
Kommst du mit? (Are you coming along?)
Ich weiß es nicht. (I do not know.)
Ich kenne ihn gut. (I know him well.)
Siehst du das? (Do you see that?)
Sprechen Sie Deutsch? (Do you speak German?)

vocabulary.english: to find / to think about sth.
vocabulary.example: Wie findest du das? (What do you think of this?)
Gibst du mir das? (Will you give me that?)
Ich nehme den Bus. (I take the bus.)
Ich brauche das nicht. (I do not need that.)
Ich arbeite heute nicht. (I am not working today.)
Ich wohne in München. (I live in Munich.)

exercises.instruction: Fill in the correct form of sein.
exercises.question: Ich ___ müde. (I am tired.)
exercises.explanation: The first-person singular of sein is bin. Full conjugation: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind.

exercises.question: How do you say 'I have to work' in German?

options.explanation: wollen = to want. This means 'I want to work'.
können = can. This means 'I can work'.
Correct! müssen = must / have to. The infinitive goes to the end.
Wrong word order! With modals: Subject + modal verb (position 2) + infinitive (end).

exercises.explanation: müssen means 'must / have to'. Structure: Subject + modal verb + [rest of sentence] + infinitive at the END.

exercises.question: Which sentence correctly uses wissen vs. kennen?

options.explanation: wissen is NOT used for people. Use kennen: Ich kenne ihn gut.

options.text: Ich kenne, dass er krank ist.
options.explanation: kennen is NOT used with dass-clauses. Use wissen: Ich weiß, dass er krank ist.
Correct! kennen is used for places, people, and things you are familiar with.
wissen is for factual knowledge (Ich weiß, dass...), not familiarity with places.

exercises.explanation: wissen = knowing facts/information (followed by clauses or es). kennen = being familiar with a person, place, or thing.

exercises.question: 'Ich muss nicht kommen' means 'I must not come'.

options.explanation: This is a very common trap! muss nicht means 'do not have to', NOT 'must not'.
Correct! 'Ich muss nicht kommen' = I do not have to come. 'I must not come' = Ich darf nicht kommen.

exercises.explanation: muss nicht = do not have to (no obligation). darf nicht = must not / not allowed to (prohibition). This is one of the most critical distinctions in A1 German.

lessons.title: 10 Core Nouns and Their Articles
lessons.shortDescription: Master the 10 highest-frequency German nouns with their grammatical gender, plurals, and everyday usage.

sections.title: Why Articles Matter So Much in German
sections.content: In German, every noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). Unlike French or Spanish, German gender cannot be reliably predicted from meaning alone — it must be memorized with the noun. Professional learners always learn nouns together with their article: not just 'Haus' but 'das Haus', not just 'Familie' but 'die Familie'. One powerful rule: nouns ending in -ung are always feminine (die) — die Wohnung, die Zeitung, die Lösung.

sections.title: The 10 Most Common German Nouns
rows: Ich habe keine Zeit. (I have no time.)
Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch. (I have been learning German for a year.)
Die Menschen hier sind nett. (The people here are nice.)
Ich gehe zur Arbeit. (I am going to work.)
Das Haus ist groß. (The house is big.)
Ich suche eine Wohnung. (I am looking for an apartment.)
Meine Familie wohnt in Berlin. (My family lives in Berlin.)
Das ist mein Freund. (This is my friend / boyfriend.)
Die Kinder spielen draußen. (The children are playing outside.)

sections.title: Mensch vs. Person — Two Words for 'Person'
sections.content: der Mensch (plural: die Menschen) emphasizes the human being — used naturally in everyday speech and philosophically: Die Menschen in Deutschland... (The people in Germany...). die Person (plural: die Personen) is more neutral and administrative: Wie viele Personen? (How many persons?). In everyday conversational German, Mensch is significantly more common.

sections.title: der Freund — Context Changes the Meaning
sections.content: der Freund has two meanings: a male friend OR a boyfriend, depending entirely on context. Das ist mein Freund could mean either 'This is my friend' or 'This is my boyfriend'. To clarify, Germans say mein bester Freund (my best friend) for platonic friendship. The female equivalent is die Freundin, which similarly means female friend or girlfriend. This ambiguity confuses learners — context always resolves it.

sections.title: Haus vs. Wohnung — House vs. Apartment
sections.content: das Haus is a standalone house with its own entrance and garden. die Wohnung is an apartment or flat within a larger building. In German cities, the vast majority of people live in Wohnungen. When someone asks Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?), a typical city answer is: Ich wohne in einer Wohnung in München-Schwabing.

sections.title: These 10 Nouns in Conversation
sections.content: — Wo wohnst du? — Ich wohne in einer Wohnung in München. Das Haus ist alt, aber die Wohnung ist schön. — Hast du Familie hier? — Ja, meine Familie und meine Freunde wohnen alle hier. Ich habe auch zwei Kinder. — Und wie ist die Arbeit? — Gut, aber ich habe wenig Zeit. Der Arbeitstag ist lang. Dieses Jahr möchte ich mehr Zeit für meine Familie haben.

vocabulary.example: Ich habe keine Zeit. (I have no time.)
Guten Tag! (Good day!)
Dieses Jahr lerne ich Deutsch. (This year I am learning German.)
Die Menschen hier sind freundlich. (The people here are friendly.)
Ich gehe zur Arbeit. (I am going to work.)
Das Haus ist sehr groß. (The house is very big.)
Ich suche eine Wohnung. (I am looking for an apartment.)
Meine Familie wohnt hier. (My family lives here.)
Das ist mein Freund Klaus. (This is my friend Klaus.)
Die Kinder spielen draußen. (The children play outside.)

exercises.question: What is the correct article for 'Wohnung' (apartment)?

options.explanation: Wohnung is not masculine.
Correct! die Wohnung — feminine. Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine.
Wohnung is not neuter. Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine (die).

exercises.explanation: Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine (die): die Wohnung, die Zeitung, die Lösung, die Arbeit. This is one of the most reliable gender rules in German.

exercises.question: A German says: 'Das ist mein Freund.' What does this most likely mean?

options.explanation: Not always — Freund means both male friend and boyfriend depending on context.
Context matters — it could be boyfriend too.

options.text: Either 'my friend' or 'my boyfriend' — context decides
options.explanation: Correct! Freund is ambiguous. Context and relationship always clarify.
The sentence is perfectly correct German.

exercises.explanation: Freund = male friend OR boyfriend. Freundin = female friend OR girlfriend. Germans often say 'mein bester Freund' (my best friend) to clarify platonic friendship.

exercises.question: ___ Kind spielt draußen. (The child plays outside.)
exercises.hint: Kind (child) — what is its grammatical gender?
exercises.explanation: das Kind — Kind is neuter (das). Plural: die Kinder. Example: Das Kind ist müde. / Die Kinder spielen.

lessons.title: 10 Core German Adjectives
lessons.shortDescription: The 10 most frequent German adjectives — each presented with its opposite for efficient learning.

sections.title: Adjectives: the Backbone of Description
sections.content: Adjectives describe nouns. In German, adjectives can be used in two positions: after a verb (predicative) — Das ist gut. (That is good.) — or directly before a noun (attributive) — ein gutes Restaurant (a good restaurant). For A1 learners, focus first on predicative use (after sein). The 10 adjectives below cover the most essential properties you need to describe the world around you.

sections.title: The 10 Core Adjectives with Their Opposites
rows: Das Essen ist gut. (The food is good.)
Das Wetter ist schlecht. (The weather is bad.)
Die Wohnung ist groß. (The apartment is big.)
Das Kind ist noch klein. (The child is still small.)
Ich habe ein neues Handy. (I have a new phone.)
Das Haus ist sehr alt. (The house is very old.)
Das ist sehr wichtig! (That is very important!)
Die Antwort ist richtig. (The answer is correct.)
Deutsch ist nicht einfach! (German is not easy!)
Die Prüfung war schwer. (The exam was hard.)

sections.title: groß — Three Meanings in One Word
sections.content: groß is remarkably versatile: it means big (eine große Stadt — a big city), tall for people (Er ist groß — He is tall), and great/significant (ein großes Problem — a big/major problem). For buildings, use hoch (tall) instead: ein hohes Gebäude (a tall building). For people, always use groß, never hoch.

sections.title: schwer — Hard AND Heavy
sections.content: schwer has two meanings that context always disambiguates: difficult (Das ist schwer — That is difficult) and physically heavy (Der Koffer ist schwer — The suitcase is heavy). To be unambiguous when meaning 'difficult', you can use schwierig instead: Das ist schwierig.

sections.title: richtig vs. wahr — Correct vs. True
sections.content: richtig = correct, right, proper — used for answers, directions, and actions: Die Antwort ist richtig. (The answer is correct.) wahr = true in the sense of factually or emotionally true: Das ist wahr. (That is true.) Practical rule: for answers and facts in a test/conversation, use richtig. For truth about reality or reality claims, use wahr.

sections.title: These 10 Adjectives in Conversation
sections.content: — Wie ist deine neue Wohnung? — Sie ist groß und schön, aber ein bisschen alt. Das Bad ist sehr klein, aber das ist nicht so wichtig. — Und wie ist die Arbeit? — Die Arbeit ist gut, aber manchmal schwer. Es gibt viele neue Dinge zu lernen. Ist Deutsch auch schwer für dich? — Ja, Deutsch ist nicht einfach! Aber die richtigen Grundlagen zu lernen ist sehr wichtig.

vocabulary.example: Das ist sehr gut! (That is very good!)
Das Wetter ist schlecht. (The weather is bad.)
Er ist sehr groß. (He is very tall.)
Das ist ein kleines Problem. (That is a small problem.)
Ich suche eine neue Arbeit. (I am looking for a new job.)
Das Haus ist sehr alt. (The house is very old.)
Das ist sehr wichtig. (That is very important.)
Das ist richtig! (That is correct!)
Das ist ganz einfach. (That is quite simple.)
Das war sehr schwer. (That was very hard.)

exercises.question: Which adjective is the opposite of 'neu' (new)?

options.explanation: groß means big, not old.
gut means good, not old.
Correct! alt means old — the direct opposite of neu (new).
schwer means difficult or heavy, not old.

exercises.explanation: Learn adjective opposites as pairs: neu/alt, gut/schlecht, groß/klein, richtig/falsch, einfach/schwer.

exercises.question: How do you say 'The answer is correct' in German?

options.explanation: wahr means 'true' (factually true), not 'correct'.
Correct! richtig = correct/right — used for answers and proper usage.
wichtig means important, not correct.
gut means good, not specifically correct.

exercises.explanation: richtig = correct/right (answers, directions, behavior). wahr = true (facts about reality). Die Antwort ist richtig. vs. Das ist wahr.

exercises.question: In German, 'groß' can describe both a big city and a tall person.

options.explanation: Correct! eine große Stadt (a big city) and Er ist groß (He is tall) — both use groß.
Actually true! groß works for size (objects) AND height (people).

exercises.explanation: groß = big (objects/places) AND tall (people). For buildings, use hoch (tall): ein hohes Gebäude. But for people: Er ist groß (He is tall).

lessons.title: 20 Essential Adverbs of Time, Degree & Place
lessons.shortDescription: Ranks 41–60: adverbs for when (heute, immer, nie), how much (sehr, viel), and where (hier, dort) — all unchanging in form.

sections.title: The Good News About German Adverbs
sections.content: Adverbs never change their form in German. Unlike adjectives, they have no case endings, no gender, no plural. You learn a word once and use it everywhere. The 20 adverbs in this lesson fall into three groups: time adverbs (when?), degree and quantity adverbs (how much?), and place and manner adverbs (where? how?).

sections.title: 10 Time Adverbs (Ranks 41–50)
rows: Was machst du heute? (What are you doing today?)
heute Morgen = this morning; heute Abend = tonight
Ich komme morgen. (I will come tomorrow.)
morgen früh = tomorrow morning. Note: der Morgen (noun) = morning
Ich muss jetzt gehen. (I have to go now.)
jetzt = right now; gerade = at this very moment
Er kommt immer zu spät. (He always comes too late.)
Ich gehe oft ins Kino. (I often go to the cinema.)
Manchmal bin ich müde. (Sometimes I am tired.)
Often placed at the start of a sentence for emphasis
Ich trinke nie Alkohol. (I never drink alcohol.)
Bist du schon fertig? (Are you already done?)
Ich bin noch nicht fertig. (I am still not done.)
noch nicht = not yet; nicht mehr = no longer
Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch. (I only speak a little German.)

sections.title: schon vs. noch — A Critical Pair
sections.content: schon = already (action happened sooner than expected): Bist du schon da? (Are you already there?) noch = still (situation is ongoing): Bist du noch da? (Are you still there?) With negation, the contrast becomes stark: noch nicht = not yet (something hasn't happened but will); schon nicht mehr = no longer (something used to happen but does not now). Mastering this pair is a milestone in natural German.

sections.title: 10 Degree, Quantity & Place Adverbs (Ranks 51–60)
rows: Ich bin auch müde. (I am also tired.)
Position: right after the subject or the verb in most cases
Das ist sehr gut! (That is very good!)
sehr intensifies adjectives and other adverbs
Ich habe viel Arbeit. (I have a lot of work.)
viele (with -e) before countable plurals: viele Freunde
Ich brauche mehr Zeit. (I need more time.)
Comparative of viel; mehr und mehr = more and more
Ich habe wenig Zeit. (I have little time.)
wenige (with -e) before countable plurals: wenige Chancen
hier = at this place; hierher = to here (direction)
dort = at that place; dorthin = to there (direction)
Wir machen das zusammen. (We will do that together.)
Key word for teamwork, relationships, shared activities
Ich bin allein zu Hause. (I am alone at home.)
allein also means 'only' in formal/literary contexts
Zuerst esse ich, dann gehe ich. (First I eat, then I go.)
zuerst = first in a sequence; then comes dann (then)

sections.title: viel vs. viele — A Very Common Grammar Trap
sections.content: viel (without ending) goes before uncountable nouns and in adverbial use: viel Zeit (a lot of time), viel arbeiten (to work a lot), Das kostet viel. (That costs a lot.) viele (with -e ending) goes before countable plural nouns: viele Menschen (many people), viele Probleme (many problems). The rule: can you count individual items? Use viele. Cannot count? Use viel.

sections.title: Adverbs in a Real Conversation
sections.content: — Bist du schon fertig? — Nein, ich bin noch nicht fertig. Ich brauche noch mehr Zeit. — Du arbeitest immer so viel! — Ja, manchmal ist es zu viel. Aber heute mache ich es zusammen mit Anna, sie hilft mir hier sehr oft. — Wohnst du noch dort in Schwabing? — Nein, jetzt wohne ich hier in Mitte. Es ist viel besser — ich bin nie allein, und es gibt immer etwas zu tun.

vocabulary.example: Was machst du heute? (What are you doing today?)
Ich komme morgen. (I will come tomorrow.)
Ich muss jetzt gehen. (I have to go now.)
Er kommt immer zu spät. (He always comes too late.)
Ich gehe oft ins Kino. (I often go to the cinema.)
Manchmal bin ich müde. (Sometimes I am tired.)
Ich trinke nie Alkohol. (I never drink alcohol.)
Bist du schon fertig? (Are you already done?)
Ich bin noch hier. (I am still here.)
Ich habe nur eine Frage. (I only have one question.)
Ich bin auch müde. (I am also tired.)
Das ist sehr wichtig! (That is very important!)
Ich habe viel Arbeit. (I have a lot of work.)
Ich brauche mehr Zeit. (I need more time.)
Ich habe wenig Zeit. (I have little time.)
Ich wohne hier. (I live here.)
Er arbeitet dort. (He works there.)
Wir machen das zusammen. (We will do that together.)
Ich bin allein zu Hause. (I am alone at home.)
Zuerst kommt die Arbeit. (Work comes first.)

exercises.question: What does 'Bist du noch hier?' mean?

options.explanation: That would be 'Bist du schon hier?' — schon = already.
Correct! noch = still. 'Are you still here?'
That requires a verb of motion: Kommst du hierher?
That would need past tense: Warst du je hier?

exercises.explanation: noch = still (ongoing). Bist du noch hier? = Are you still here? Compare: schon = already. Bist du schon hier? = Are you already here?

exercises.question: Which is correct: 'Ich habe ___ Freunde.' (I have many friends.)

options.explanation: Freunde is a countable plural noun — use viele, not viel.
Correct! viele is used with countable plural nouns.
sehr means 'very' and modifies adjectives and adverbs, not nouns directly.
mehr means 'more' (comparative), not 'many'.

exercises.explanation: viel = much/a lot (uncountable: viel Zeit, viel Arbeit). viele = many (countable plurals: viele Freunde, viele Menschen).

exercises.question: Er kommt ___ zu spät. (He always comes too late.)
exercises.explanation: immer = always. The frequency scale: immer (always) — oft (often) — manchmal (sometimes) — selten (rarely) — nie (never).

lessons.title: Conjunctions, Prepositions & Essential Phrases
lessons.shortDescription: Ranks 61–100: the grammar words that link ideas, the 12 most common prepositions, and 20 survival phrases every learner must know.

sections.title: Conjunctions: The Architecture of German Sentences
sections.content: Conjunctions connect sentences and clauses. German has two types with critically different effects on word order. Coordinating conjunctions (und, oder, aber) connect two main clauses and do NOT change word order — the verb remains in position 2. Subordinating conjunctions (weil, dass, wenn) introduce a subordinate clause and send the conjugated verb to the VERY END of that clause. This verb-final rule is one of the defining characteristics of German sentence structure.

sections.title: 8 Essential Conjunctions (Ranks 61–68)
rows: Ich arbeite und lerne Deutsch. (I work and learn German.) — normal word order
Kaffee oder Tee? (Coffee or tea?) — normal word order
Ich will kommen, aber ich habe keine Zeit. (I want to come, but I have no time.) — normal word order
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland wohne. (I learn German because I live in Germany.) — verb to END
Ich weiß, dass er kommt. (I know that he is coming.) — verb to END
Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich. (If I have time, I will come.) — verb to END; main verb inverts after wenn-clause
Zuerst arbeite ich, dann gehe ich. (First I work, then I go.) — causes inversion: dann + verb + subject
Ich bin müde, also gehe ich nach Hause. (I am tired, so I am going home.) — causes inversion

sections.title: weil and dass Always Push the Verb to the End
sections.content: This is the most important word order rule for subordinate clauses. Compare: Ich gehe nach Hause. (verb in position 2) vs. weil ich nach Hause gehe. (verb at the END — because I am going home). And: Ich weiß, dass er nach Hause geht. (I know that he is going home — geht is at the end). This structure is called Verbendstellung (verb-final position) and is non-negotiable in standard German.

sections.title: The 12 Most Essential German Prepositions
sections.content: German prepositions determine the grammatical case of the noun that follows them. Some always take Akkusativ (für, ohne, gegen), some always take Dativ (mit, von, nach, bei), and some are two-way prepositions that take Akkusativ for direction/movement and Dativ for location/state (über, unter, vor, hinter, zwischen). At A1 level, focus on learning the prepositions with their most common meanings.

sections.title: 12 Core Prepositions (Ranks 69–80)
rows: Ich fahre mit dem Bus. (I am going by bus.)
Das ist für dich. (That is for you.)
Ich komme von der Arbeit. (I am coming from work.)
Ich fahre nach Berlin. (I am going to Berlin.)
Ich bin bei meiner Freundin. (I am at my girlfriend's place.)
Wir sprechen über die Arbeit. (We are talking about work.)
Das Buch liegt unter dem Tisch. (The book is under the table.)
Er steht vor dem Haus. (He is standing in front of the house.)
Das Auto steht hinter dem Haus. (The car is behind the house.)
Die Bank liegt zwischen dem Supermarkt und der Post. (The bank is between the supermarket and the post office.)
Ich komme gegen 8 Uhr. (I will come around 8 o'clock.)

sections.title: nach vs. in vs. zu — Getting the Destination Right
sections.content: Choosing the right preposition for travel destinations is one of the most common A1 challenges. Use nach for cities and most countries (no article): nach Berlin, nach Deutschland, nach Hause. Use in for countries that require an article: in die Türkei, in den Iran, in die USA. Use zu for people and specific local destinations: zum Arzt (to the doctor), zur Arbeit (to work), zu meiner Freundin (to my girlfriend's place). These three cover virtually every destination scenario.

sections.title: Essential German Phrases (Ranks 81–100)
sections.content: These 20 words and expressions are the social oil that keeps every German conversation flowing. They are the first words you need to understand and the first ones native speakers will direct at you. Knowing them fluently — without hesitation — signals respect and basic competence in German-speaking environments.

sections.title: 20 Essential Phrases & Expressions (Ranks 81–100)
rows: Simple agreement. Ja? = Really? (surprised or asking for confirmation)
Direct refusal. Nein, danke = No, thank you.
please / you're welcome / here you go / pardon?
4 uses: please (request), you're welcome (after danke), here you go (handing sth.), pardon? (did not hear)
Danke schön = Thank you very much. Danke sehr = Thank you very much (stronger). Vielen Dank = Many thanks.
Getting someone's attention: Entschuldigung! Starting a question: Entschuldigung, wo ist...?
Safe in almost all everyday contexts. More formal option: Guten Tag.
Used until approximately 11am. Morgen! is the short informal version between colleagues.
Very widely used across Germany. More formal: Auf Wiedersehen (Goodbye / Until we meet again).
Natürlich! = Of course! Confident agreement. Can also mean 'obviously' in context.
Ich komme vielleicht. (I might come.) Less certain than wahrscheinlich (probably).
Wirklich? = Really? (surprise). Das ist wirklich toll! (That is really great!)
Native speakers use genau constantly to confirm understanding: Genau! = Exactly! Right!
Ich trinke gern Kaffee. (I like to drink coffee.) Gern geschehen! (My pleasure! / You are welcome!)
Leider nicht. (Unfortunately not.) Ich kann leider nicht kommen. (I am afraid I cannot come.)
Ich komme sofort! (I am coming right away!) Expresses urgency or quick response.
Das ist möglich. (That is possible.) Das ist nicht möglich! (That is impossible!)
Kein Problem! (No problem!) — one of the most reassuring phrases in German.
Gute Frage! (Good question!) Ich habe eine Frage. (I have a question.)
Was ist die Antwort? (What is the answer?) Ich warte auf deine Antwort. (I am waiting for your reply.)
Zum Beispiel... (For example...) — abbreviated as z.B. in writing. Used constantly.

sections.title: bitte — The Most Versatile Word in German
sections.content: bitte is used in at least four different situations you will encounter immediately: 1) Please in requests: Einen Kaffee, bitte. (A coffee, please.) 2) You are welcome after danke: Danke! — Bitte! 3) Here you go when handing something: Hier, bitte! 4) Pardon? when you did not hear: Bitte? Learn all four — they all appear in the first week of living in a German-speaking country.

sections.title: A Complete Conversation Using Ranks 61–100
sections.content: — Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Deutsch? — Ja, natürlich. Aber ich spreche nur ein bisschen. — Kein Problem! Ich habe eine Frage: Wo ist der Bahnhof? — Hmm, ich weiß nicht genau... Er ist vielleicht dort hinten, aber ich bin nicht sicher. — Wirklich? Auf der Karte ist er hier. — Ach sofort — ich kenne die Straße! Gehen Sie geradeaus, dann links. Das ist das Beispiel: geradeaus, dann links. — Danke sehr! — Bitte! Gute Reise!

Kaffee oder Tee? (Coffee or tea?)

Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich hier wohne. (I learn German because I live here.)
Ich weiß, dass er kommt. (I know that he is coming.)

exercises.question: Which sentence uses 'weil' correctly?

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich lebe in Deutschland.
options.explanation: Wrong! After weil the verb must go to the END: weil ich in Deutschland lebe.

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil in Deutschland ich lebe.
options.explanation: Wrong word order in the weil-clause. The conjugated verb must come last.

options.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland lebe.
options.explanation: Correct! weil sends the conjugated verb (lebe) to the very end of its clause.

options.text: Weil ich in Deutschland lebe ich, lerne Deutsch.
options.explanation: Multiple errors — extra pronoun and wrong main clause order.

exercises.explanation: weil is a subordinating conjunction — it sends the conjugated verb to the END: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland LEBE. (lebe is last!)

exercises.question: How do you say 'I am going to Berlin' in German?

options.explanation: zu is used for people and local destinations (zum Arzt), not cities.
in + Akkusativ is for countries with an article (in die Türkei), not cities.
Correct! nach is used for cities and most countries (without an article).
bei means 'at / near' — not used for travel destinations.

exercises.explanation: nach for cities and most countries: nach Berlin, nach Deutschland, nach Hause. in + Akkusativ for countries with articles: in die Türkei, in die USA.

exercises.question: Someone gives you your coffee and says 'Hier, bitte!' — what do they mean?

options.explanation: Not correct in this context.
Correct! Hier, bitte! = Here you go! — bitte when presenting something means 'here you go'.
Bitte as 'you are welcome' comes AFTER someone says danke, not when handing something.
Not correct in this context.

exercises.explanation: bitte has 4 uses: 1) please (request), 2) you are welcome (after danke), 3) here you go (handing something), 4) pardon? (did not hear). Hier, bitte! = Here you go!

exercises.question: Zum ___ : Ich trinke gern Kaffee. (For example: I like to drink coffee.)
exercises.explanation: Zum Beispiel = For example. Abbreviated as z.B. in formal writing. One of the most useful phrases in academic, professional, and everyday German.
